title: Sports Metaphors in the English Classroom
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart argues that a handful of sports and movie metaphors, introduced early and repeated all year, can move ninth graders to do hard literacy work. He builds three: Spartak (talent is built through myelination, feedback and attention to weakness), the montage mirage (teens mistake a movie training montage for the real length of effort) and Karate Kid's jacket on, jacket off (repetition of sentence templates builds fluency). Each metaphor is tied to a concrete classroom routine such as a close reading, a clip discussion or a before-and-after debate comparison. The larger aim is student ownership of their education rather than mere engagement. The move is to give students a shared vocabulary for effort that the teacher can invoke whenever the work gets frustrating.
points: Shared metaphors give a teacher a motivational shorthand that can be reused all year when reading or writing gets hard.
The Spartak lesson uses Coyle's myelin article to let students argue for themselves that talent is developed through feedback-rich practice.
The montage mirage names a specific teenage misbelief: that brief, intense effort is enough to prepare for college and career.
Showing students their own early and late debate clips makes the payoff of repetitive template practice visible.
quotes: The article explores the science around a fatty substance called myelin — a substance so significant that Coyle claims myelin is essentially talent itself. Here’s how it works: when specific neural pathways are used repeatedly — say, the pathway used when serving a tennis ball — a myelin sheath forms around the pathway, and this sheath acts like the rubber coating around an electrical cord.

I tell them that the majority of teenagers in the USA have watched too many sports movies and are unable to properly “read” them; essentially, they believe that the montage scenes are literal, and that, if they’ll just work hard for a few minutes, earbuds blasting in their ears, they’ll be ready for the reading and writing demands of college/career.

I don’t think teenagers literally misunderstand that montage scenes represent a long period of hard work. Instead, I do think most teenagers believe they need not work hard to prepare to live flourishing lives.

However, simply stopping here wouldn’t be as powerful as showing them how far they’ve come, so I play a clip from their first in-class debate of the school year. I then have them compare that to their performance in a more recent debate, excerpts of which we also watch.

But my goal here is not simply that they’ll like my class or be engaged while in it — it’s that they’ll own their education. As freshmen in high school, they all have a chance to make just about whatever they want of their lives, but if they’re not careful, mistakes in ninth grade can begin to delete options from their future pretty quickly.
Why? Because as I tell them, we are a team in a game called Life Domination. The game is huge, complex, and dangerous.
